title: Beware of Greeks bearing gifts
author: Vergil
setting: Troy, before the city falls: Laocoön warns the Trojans

edition.name: The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil, edited by J. B. Greenough (Boston: Ginn and Company, 1881), public domain; the Perseus Digital Library TEI text (PerseusDL canonical-latinLit, phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2), whose header credits "J. B. Greenough", "Ginn and Company", "1881"
edition.section: Aeneid 2.48-49 (the last two lines of Laocoön's speech, 2.42-49)

source_text:
aut aliquis latet error; equo ne credite, Teucri.
Quicquid id est, timeo Danaos et dona ferentis.
excerpt_note: Two lines, as printed by Greenough (who capitalizes Quicquid and spells ferentis). Laocoön's speech begins at 2.42; the Perseus file marks it as quoted speech but prints no quotation marks.

macrons.note: Macrons are editorial: added by Vocābula, not printed in the edition. Vowel quantities follow the app lexicon (Wheelock / DCC spellings) where the word is in it, and standard dictionary quantities otherwise.
uncertain: ferentīs: accusative plural in -īs (long ī), the spelling Greenough prints; other editions print ferentēs with the same quantity in -ēs.
Danaōs: Danaī has a short first a (Dănăī); the macron marks only the long ending; not machine-checked.
Teucrī: the first syllable is long (diphthong eu); only the ending carries a macron.
crēdite: short i (third conjugation); not machine-checked.

tokens.parse: nom. sg. m. (used as an adjective with error)
pres. participle, acc. pl. m. (-īs, an older spelling of -ēs)

translation: Or some other trick is lurking: do not trust the horse, Trojans. Whatever it is, I fear the Greeks even when they come bearing gifts.
translation_note: et here means "even", not "and": the Greeks are to be feared even as givers of gifts. Danaī ("Danaans") is one of Vergil's names for the Greeks. ferentīs is the accusative plural of the present participle; Greenough's -īs is an older spelling of -ēs, and other editions print ferentēs.

essay.t: Book 2 of the Aeneid is Aeneas' own story, told at the request of the queen of Carthage: the last night of Troy.
The Greeks have built a horse as big as a mountain, hidden armed men inside, and pretended to sail home, while really waiting off the island of Tenedos.

Laocoön runs down from the citadel with a crowd and warns the Trojans: either Greeks are hidden in the wood, or the horse is an engine against the walls, or some other trick is lurking; whatever it is, he fears the Greeks even when they bring gifts.
Then he hurls a spear into the horse's side, and the hollow belly groans.
Aeneas adds that if the gods' decrees and the Trojans' own minds had not been set against it, Troy would still be standing.
Instead the Greek Sinon arrives with a false story, and two serpents come over the sea from Tenedos and kill Laocoön and his two sons at the altar.
The Trojans take this as punishment for striking the sacred wood, and they breach their own walls to bring the horse in.
Versions differ: Vergil has him serving as Neptune's priest by lot; in other accounts, as in Britannica's summary, he is Apollo's priest, and his punishment is explained in other ways.

The story is also famous in marble: the Laocoön group in the Vatican was found on the Esquiline Hill in 1506 and identified with a work Pliny the Elder ascribed to sculptors of Rhodes; the museum dates it to around 40 to 30 BC, but the date is debated.
The English proverb "Beware of Greeks bearing gifts" is a loose version: Laocoön says only that he fears them, and et means "even".
Editions differ in small ways, too: Greenough prints Quicquid and ferentis, and the Dickinson College Commentaries print Quidquid and ferentēs.
For a reader working toward the whole Aeneid, line 49 is an inviting start: it is short, it is famous, and words like timeō, dōna, id and est are already in this app.

questions.q: What does et mean in timeō Danaōs et dōna ferentīs?
What does Laocoön do right after his warning?
options: He hurls a spear into the horse's side
He climbs inside the horse to search it
He flees from the city with his sons
He sacrifices the horse to Neptune

questions.q: In Vergil, whose priest is Laocoön (in other accounts he serves Apollo)?
